title: Why León tastes the way it does

lede.text: On a summer day in León the days can be very hot, and the night is much colder. That swing builds the natural acidity behind the fresh rosés of Prieto Picudo.

chapters.title: A cold plateau at the foot of the mountains
paras: León sits in the cold version of the Mediterranean climate. The Atlantic and the north should soften its temperatures and bring plenty of rain. But the plateau is high and lies at the edge of the Cordillera Cantábrica, so the climate turns continental instead.
Vines for quality wine stop at 900 m. Above that, ripening can be irregular.

fly.label: Edge of the Cordillera Cantábrica
fly.caption: The mountain edge that, with the high plateau, makes León's climate continental.

chapters.title: Hot days, cold nights
paras: Winter is harsh and long, with fog and frost. Even so, the lowest temperatures in the coldest months never pass -15°C, the limit for vines in winter. Spring is irregular, with mild spells and spring frosts. They are never a limiting factor for growing vines. Summer alternates very hot, arid spells with cold ones, and the warmest months always average above 20°C. Autumn is mild and a little rainy, which helps the grapes finish ripening.
About 500 mm of rain falls in a year, spread over summer and autumn. Vines need no irrigation except in a few isolated years. The sun shines about 2,700 hours a year.

That light feeds the leaves and berries, so they gather sugars and polyphenols. The polyphenols give rosés and reds their intense, warm colours. The gap between very hot days and much colder nights lets the vine carry out the cell respiration that builds its natural acidity, about 5.5 g/l of tartaric acid in the must. That is the freshness of León's rosés. Hot days also help the skins build up the terpenes that carry Prieto Picudo's aroma.

chapters.title: Stones, gravel and little else
paras: The soils all lie below 900 m and fall into three groups. The first is the rañas, a flat plateau of coarse rolled stones in a sandy, silty matrix. It slopes south from 1,000 m to 800 m. The rivers Órbigo, Esla and Cea have worn it into small hills. These soils are poor in fertility and organic matter. Stones run through the whole profile, so air and drainage are good.

The second group is the terraces, laid down by the Esla, Órbigo and Cea as they eroded and deposited gravel. They hold pebbles, gravel and sand, with a little silt and clay. The vineyard has traditionally sat here. Their drainage is excellent and they keep an acceptable amount of water. They are deep and poor in organic matter. The big quality denominations of Castilla y León mostly sit on this type of soil.

The third group is the campiña, a gently rolling land that covers Los Oteros and Tierra de Campos. Tierra de Campos has finer soils of marl, clay, sandstone and calcareous conglomerate. Los Oteros is coarser, with less clay.

Every one of these soils is low in organic matter, and that matters most for the whites. The whites are very aromatic because the soils under them are especially light, with little clay and excellent drainage.

fly.label: Terraces of the Esla at Valdevimbre
fly.caption: The Esla terraces, where the vineyard has traditionally sat, include the whole Valdevimbre zone.

fly.label: Tierra de Campos
fly.caption: Gently rolling campiña, with finer soils of marl, clay and sandstone than Los Oteros.

chapters.title: Whole bunches in the rosé
paras: Prieto Picudo, the main grape, gives an irregular crop. Long pruning suits it best: it is most productive from the fourth and fifth bud on each cane. New plantings of the past 20 years have all been on trellises, and the rules let trellised vines yield more grapes.

One rosé technique is found only in this zone. It is called madreo. The winemaker adds whole, perfectly healthy Prieto Picudo bunches, 5 to 10% of the tank's capacity, to rosé fermenting in the tank. When fermentation ends, the bunches are thrown away. The rosé gains deeper colour and more structure. A fine bubble of natural carbon dioxide, from the physical and chemical processes of the technique, adds more freshness. Many wineries make a classic rosé and also set aside some must for madreo.

Young Prieto Picudo reds are intense in colour, aroma and taste. They have red and black fruit, above all red fruit such as strawberry and raspberry. They are fleshy and full-bodied, with some astringency and a long finish. Reds aged in oak barrels add wood and toast to the fruit. Whites of Albarín are more aromatic than those of Verdejo or Godello, but they have less complexity and structure. More and more wineries blend Albarín with Verdejo or age it in barrel to give it more.

A wine may name a single municipality on the label only if 85% of its grapes come from vineyards in that municipality.
